body: Industrialization and Technology meet Art According to Frank Popper, “one can only speak of the direct influence of technology on art since the Industrial Revolution, and more particularly when its effects entered everyday life at the end of the 19th century through the progressive design movements known as Art Nouveau and its precedent, the Arts and Crafts movement, in England.” The first world’s fair, The Great Exhibition of London, kicks off the Modern Era of our Timeline due to its association with industrialization and its impact on the Arts and Crafts movement. The fair captured a world on the brink of a paradigm shift, the beginning of a new era in which technology and art would join and grow ever closer. Organized by Henry Cole, the legendary founder of the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the fair’s showcase of poorly crafted manufactured goods with ornate Victorian design inspired backlash in the form of England’s Arts and Crafts movement. The event would inspire Arts & Crafts artists and designers to incorporate craftsmanship and traditional techniques into new technologies, ultimately leading to the development of both modern graphic and industrial design. In the coming decades, Arts and Crafts would usher in the era of technology impacting art which led to Art Nouveau and the Bauhaus. This moment is thus the spark that lit the fuse of the modern era of generative art with its criticisms, adjustments to and embrace of rapidly industrializing societies and new technologies in art.

cite.label: Popper, Frank. Art of the Electronic Age, 10. New York: Thames and Hudson, 1997.

body: In what Hans Ulrich Obrist considers the birth of Modernism, Gustave Courbet erected—at his own expense—the Pavilion of Realism in 1855, eight years prior to the Salon des Refusés. Courbet’s earlier rejection of Salon authority came after his works were excluded from the official Salon following a public dispute with Comte Nieuwerkerke, its influential superintendent of fine arts. The exhibition was either a bold act of defiance against the restrictive artistic norms of his time or the result of a petty beef. It was intentionally set directly adjacent to the prestigious Universal Exposition in Paris from which Courbet’s work was also rejected due to his spat with Nieuwerkerke. Within his Pavilion, Courbet showcased The Painter’s Studio, a monumental painting that exemplified his commitment to portraying the truth of contemporary life. Along with it was the equally scandalous masterpiece, A Burial at Ornans. Obrist explains the importance of the exhibition: “Courbet’s self-mounted exhibition inaugurated the modern period in painting, in which the artist, rather than [their] patron, became the protagonist of art.” [Ways of Curating, 37]

cite.label: Mainardi, Patricia. "Courbet's Exhibitionism." Gazette des Beaux-Arts 118 (December 1991): 253-265.

body: The iconic firm was modeled on a craftsman’s workshop and took a pioneering stand against the non-functional role ascribed to art. The firm specialized in wallpaper designs with natural imagery but grew to manufacture furniture, textiles and stained glass as well. It stressed handcrafted production over the use of machine. Another important concept developed by Morris Co. was that the artist (or designer) should take a holistic approach, becoming involved in the entire creative process. These innovations would prove greatly influential to the upcoming Arts & Crafts movement. According to Frank Popper, this firm and the related Arts & Crafts movement were foundational in the development of the Bauhaus and even digital art, textile design and wallpaper patterns.

body: In what some consider to be the birth of Modernism in art, Manet’s Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe was flatly rejected by the Paris Salon for its unconventional style and subject matter. The painting, featuring a nude woman picnicking with clothed men, was considered scandalous at the time, as the nude woman was no longer cloaked under the legitimacy of Salon-approved topics such as mythology or history. This rejection prompted the state to open the Salon des Refusés, a monumental event in art history which kicked off the yet-to-be-named Impressionism movement. Some also consider this birth of Modernism but countering theories exist such as the Courbet’s Pavilion of Realism or my own that begins this chapter (the London World’s Fair of 1851). The industrialization and cultural conditions of the previous century gave rise to art based on personal experiences and non-realistic depictions of the world. A new avant-garde emerged that would go on to radically change the world of art for the next century.

cite.label: Desnoyers, Fernand. Le Salon des Refuses: La peinture en 1863. Paris: Azur Dutil, 1863.

body: The “exhibition of rejects,” a response to the rejection of many artists' works by the official Salon in Paris, begins. Since 1667, the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture held public exhibitions for their standout students. This exhibition came to be known as the Salon. For artists rejected from the conservative Salon’s jury, it meant patrons would be nearly impossible to find. In 1863, there was uproar after the jury selections and it took Emperor Napoleon III to order a separate exhibition to be organized for these rejected works. The simultaneous exhibition was called the Salon des Refusés (“Exhibition of the Rejects”). The Salon des Refusés featured the work of Manet, Cézanne and Pissarro yet the critical reception was poor with visitors only attending to ridicule the event. The exhibition radically challenged the established norms of the art world, sparking debates and paving the way for new artistic movements like Impressionism. The Salon des Refusés not only challenged the authority of the Salon jury but also contributed to a broader redefinition of artistic expression, marking a significant shift towards modern art and challenging traditional academic standards.

body: James Clerk Maxwell’s “On Governors”, his theoretical analysis of Watt’s governor published in 1867 and 1868, a device used for regulating the speed of steam engines, was a significant contribution to the understanding of feedback control systems. It stands as a foundational moment in the history of cybernetics, as mentioned in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog.

This epochal event in art history, held in Paris, marked the emergence of the Impressionist movement, which challenged the cultural monopoly of the Paris Salon and paved the way for modern art. The exhibition was organized by a group calling themselves the “Anonymous Cooperative Society of Artists.” It featured around 175 works by 30 artists such as Monet, Renoir and Degas. The show was generally regarded as a failure, receiving infamously hostile reviews and poor attendance. There would be eight Impressionism exhibitions in total running from 1874 to 1886.

Critic Louis Leroy gave the Impressionist movement its name when he accused Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise of being merely a sketch or “impression.” This was meant as insult by Leroy as it implied that Monet’s work was not a finished painting.

The Second Impressionist Exhibition, held in Paris, was important in consolidating the Impressionist movement as a group and distinct style. Organized by the same anonymous cooperative as the first, the second exhibition featured 250 pieces by around 20 artists, including Monet’s The Japanese Girl and Caillebotte’s The Floor Planers. Still heavily ridiculed, the second exhibition actually generated enough in sales to cover costs and pay each artist a token amount.

Designed by William Morris and woven for Morris & Co. by the Heckmondwike Manufacturing Company, this was the first dateable Morris design for a woven furnishing textile, important for its budding abstraction. The piece features grid-like, symmetrical repeating patterns of natural forms, anticipating the upcoming Art Nouveau movement’s use of nature as well as as the early digital generative art structure. The work, as well as Morris & Co.’s growing interior design innovations were emblematic of what would become known as the Arts & Crafts movement. Art Nouveau and Arts & Crafts, both progressive design movements, were some of the earliest examples of how technology began influencing art during the first wave of industrialization.

cite.label: Popper, Frank. Art of the Electronic Age, 10. New York: Thames and Hudson, 1997.

body: James Whistler’s Peacock Room stands as an important example in the history of installation and immersive art, which has a rich tradition in digital art. But the room is also a an episode of art exceeding the bounds of commission, James McNeill Whistler transformed Frederick Leyland’s dining room into what would become known as the Peacock Room, originally intended as minor touch-ups by the artist while architect Thomas Jeckyll was ill. Upon Leyland’s return, he discovered that Whistler had radically altered the space, painting over expensive leather wall coverings and embellishing the room with lavish gold and blue-green peacock motifs. The transformation culminated in Whistler adding a mural titled Art and Money; or, The Story of the Room, featuring two peacocks in a standoff, symbolizing the tension between artist and patron over the financial value of artistic labor. Hans Ulrich Obrist explains the rooms importance further: “It prefigured installation art, in which an artist works on the entire environment of a space, rather that simply decorating a part of it with a painting or sculpture.”

body: One of the world’s first commercially successful typewriters, the Remington and Sons Standard Number 2 typewriter featured a QWERTY keyboard, which it helped to establish as the standard to this day. Its introduction revolutionized written communication. The typewriter would allow and inspire artists to create intricate, repetitive and pattern-based compositions through typed characters, offering a precursor to the digital generative art of today. The typewriter’s influence on artistic expression, particularly in the realms of concrete poetry and text-based art, helped shape the trajectory of generative art by introducing the concept of using machines and rules to generate visually striking and conceptually layered compositions.

body: The term “art nouveau” first appeared in the 1880s in the Belgian journal L’Art Moderne to describe the work of Les Vingt. A significant moment in the history of modern art, Art Nouveau was characterized by intricate, flowing lines and organic, natural forms. It revolutionized the approach to architecture, furniture and graphic design, making use of the technological innovations of the turn of the century. Art Nouveau was an important precursor to modernism, which emphasized function over form and the elimination of superfluous ornament. Influenced by the ideas of the Arts & Crafts movement, Art Nouveau designers and artists sought to synthesize art and craft. The styles were similar as well with both emphasizing nature and the Gothic style. Both were interested in architecture and design’s power to reshape the human environment and, thus, experience.

Seurat begins his best-known painting, A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, completed in 1886. This seminal work of Post-Impressionism is known for its innovative use of pointillism, “a highly systematic and scientific technique based on the hypothesis that closely positioned points of pure color mix together in the viewer’s eye.” It also exemplifies the movement’s interest in depicting people from different social classes’ everyday life through a modern, formalist lens.

body: Founded in London and born out of the influence of William Morris and Philip Webb, the society’s objective was “to assert a new public relevance for the work of decorative artists.” Arts & Crafts sought to erase the distinction between fine art, design and craft, while uniting creativity and manufacturing. The society also officially gave the Arts & Crafts movement its name. This progressive design movement was one of the first to pose questions about the latest technology, mechanization and art. Arts & Crafts sought to harmonize the relationship between the artist, machines and art. Morris’s philosophical stand against poorly made manufactured goods would prove highly influential to Henry van de Velde, who brought Art Nouveau to Belgium and founded the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts. Walter Gropius would take over for van de Velde and the Arts and Crafts school would become the Bauhaus in 1919. Thus, a line can be drawn from the ideas of Morris directly to the founding of Bauhaus. Morris and this enormously important movement, according to Frank Popper, is the beginning of electronic art’s journey.

body: English logician and mathematician John Venn constructed “a very fair graphical indication of randomness,” according to himself in the third edition of his seminal book, The Logic of Chance. A precursor to generative art and systemic art and thinking, Venn’s illustration consisted of a single, simple rule: Draw “a line which at every instant is as likely to take one direction as another.” From this simple rule, infinite possibilities of randomness can occur and a basic generative system was born. This book also ties together earlier moments in Chapter 1 that discuss logic and the visualization of mathematics. Here, Venn combines the two to visualize rules or as they’re more commonly referred to today, algorithms.

These annual exhibitions by the newly formed Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society aimed to raise the cultural standing and awareness of craft work, such as ceramics, textiles, metalwork and furniture. According to the V&A, “for many years in Britain exhibitions mounted by the Society were the only public platform for the decorative arts, and were critical in changing the way people looked at manufactured objects.”

body: Henri Poincaré's work in the late 19th and early 20th century laid the foundation for the modern science of chaos and complexity, which has been critically influential on computer and generative art. The well-known three body problem concerned the difficulty of predicting the position of three celestial bodies in close proximity to another. Poincaré did not actually solve the problem but he did discover the butterfly effect which gave rise to the new field of chaos theory in the 1960s.

The exhibition at Ambroise Vollard’s gallery in Paris was significant for establishing Cézanne as a major artist of his time. The exhibition introduced Cézanne’s innovative style of using simplified forms and flattened space, laying the groundwork for the development of modern art’s journey to abstraction and movements such as Cubism.

This poem was one of the very first intimate and intense marriages of free verse and typographic freedom. It served as the precursor not only to twentieth-century avant-garde poetics (from Futurists and Constructivists, via Appolinarie and Dada to Surrealists then later to Visual, Concrete…) but also the birthplace of the artist’s book as well as concept albums. -Vuk Ćosić

body: German architect Hermann Muthesius, posted to London from 1896, was influenced by the Arts and Crafts Movement, including the latest developments in art and architecture. He brought ideas back to Germany, such as the importance of traditional craftsmanship, simplicity of design and the integration of art into everyday life. Muthesius would found the Deutscher Werkbund which had a major influence on Walter Gropius, founder of the Bauhaus and Le Corbusier. This explains how the ideas of the Arts & Crafts movement via Muthesius would go on to shape our concepts of art, architecture and design to this day.

cite.label: Derbal, Mohamed. "The London Exchange: Hermann Muthesius and the Transnational Creation of National Identities, 1896-1903." arq: Architectural Research Quarterly 28, no. 4 (2024): 361-374.

body: The shocking exhibition held in Paris at the Salon d’Automne, featured Fauvist work characterized by bold and experimental use of color, including Henri Matisse’s Woman with a Hat. Fauvism opened the door for more extreme approaches to abstraction. Artists, such as Matisse, innovated with color, inspiring countless others, including Kandinsky’s Blue Rider Group, Color Field painters and Expressionists. The movement’s incorporation of impulse and spontaneity also led the way for greater experimentation with randomness in art. This laid the groundwork for artists to further explore non-representational forms, where chance and randomness could play an even more prominent role.

Beginning in the 1870s by the “Father of Post-Impressionism,” this series of forty-five watercolor and thirty-six oil paintings would have an outsized impact on art history. Significant for their challenging approach to landscape paintings, Cézanne broke from traditional conventions by flattening the space and using repeated forms to create a sense of depth. Cézanne famously believed that painters should “treat nature by means of the cylinder, the sphere, the cone,” one of the first breaths of abstraction in arts modernization. Cézanne also portrayed his subject matter, in this case Mont Sainte-Victoire, from diverse angles and points of view, highly influencing Picasso and Georges Braque’s development of Cubism. “His innovations were tremendously influential for the masters of modernity, like Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso. Picasso even went so far as to call Cézanne ‘the father of us all.’”

Cubism, one of the most influential movements of the twentieth century and inspired by Cézanne’s use of basic geometric shapes, is born with Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon. The painting preceded Picasso’s partnership with Georges Braque, who saw it later in 1907. Les Demoiselles is proto-Cubist. The first phase proper, Analytical Cubism, ran from 1908 to 1912, when Picasso and Braque broke objects down into their basic geometrical shapes, extending the ideas of Cézanne nearly to their logical conclusions. Cubism “brought different views of subjects (usually objects or figures) together in the same picture, resulting in paintings that appear fragmented and abstracted.” This marked a revolutionary departure from the Renaissance tradition of the illusion of space created from linear perspective. Cubism was not only a monumental step in modern art’s abstraction, it was crucial to digital generative art’s development as well. For instance, beyond its embrace of geometric forms, Cubism introduced a temporal, fourth dimension to visual art by presenting multiple perspectives of an object in a single composition. This shattered the notion of a fixed viewpoint and suggested the passage of time and movement within the artwork, anticipating Op and Kinetic art, two key predecessors of digital generative art.

body: Monumental works in the history of abstraction, Swedish artist Hilma af Klint created abstract paintings before the term “abstract art” was even coined. Group IV, The Ten Largest, No. 7, Adulthood is one of her most significant works, part of a series of ten large-scale paintings. The paintings are largely influenced the ideas of spiritualism and Theosophy, which were popular in the Western world at the time. The pieces challenge the Western art historical canon, pre-dating the work of male artists like Kandinsky and Mondrian who are typically credited with the invention of abstract art. Thus, the works are representative of the challenges women artists have faced throughout history. These colossal works in art history were kept privately underground for decades and rarely exhibited. Af Klint even stipulated in her will that the paintings could not be shown for twenty years after her passing. They would be essentially lost and forgotten until 1986. In 1988, The Secret Paintings of Hilma af Klint toured around Finland, Iceland and Norway in a small exhibition. New York’s P.S.1 Contemporary Art Center showcased the works a year later in 1989 which finally drew broader public attention to the works. Af Klint’s work consistently toured around Europe for the next several decades but it was not until 2018 that af Klint received a major solo exhibition in the United States, Hilma af Klint: Paintings for the Future at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.

body: The Deutscher Werkbund in Munich, a crucially important and influential association, aimed at improving German design and industry in global markets by partnering product manufacturers with design professionals. Muthesius found inspiration for the Werkbund from his time spent in England, particularly from his time absorbing the Arts & Crafts movement. A member of the Werkbund, Walter Gropius, would advance the principles of the Werkbund further by later creating the Bauhaus school of design. Considered by Frank Popper instrumental in the development of digital art, the Werkbund also played a significant role in shaping modernist design principles, promoting the use of industrial production methods with traditional crafts.

body: The radical and provocative first exhibition of the Blue Rider Group, founded by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, was a significant development in the abstraction of art. Influenced by Fauvism especially, the works emphasized color, form and spirituality over artistic tradition.

Inspired by the ideas of Cubism and Futurism, Sonia and Robert Delaunay sought with Orphism to create a new kind of abstract art. Their work emphasized the interplay of color and light, often using circular forms and contrasting hues to create dynamic visual effects. A key development in modern art’s abstraction, Orphism likened painting to music. Its musical inspiration explain the movement’s interest in expressing dynamism, inspiring future movements to embrace visual rhythms, optical effects and other dynamic relationship between elements, including digital generative art. These movements include Op art and Kinetic art, two important predecessors of electronic art.

Deeply influenced by William Morris’s Arts and Crafts philosophy, Belgian architect and designer Henry van de Velde combined the Arts and Crafts School and the Academy of Fine Arts of Weimar to form the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts. Van de Velde would be rather short-lived in his tenure due to the approaching WWI. The impact of the school on human history, however, was profound. The school sought a harmonious solution to the problems posed at all levels of a rapidly modernizing life, specifically the machine-artisan-art triad. The school also attempted to articulate a socially committed, scientific aesthetic. Walter Gropius would later succeed van de Velde who was forced to resign in 1915, one year into WWI, due to his Belgian heritage. In 1919, the school, under Gropius, would become the Bauhaus.

body: Rejected by the Cubists for appearing too Futurist, this proto-Dadaist painting applies a machine aesthetic to the human form, anticipating the dynamism of Kinetic Art that led to electronic art. Duchamp called this series of paintings “an organization of kinetic elements - an expression of time and space through the abstract presentation of movement…[But] we must bear in mind that, when we consider the movement of form in space over a certain time, we are entering the realm of geometry and mathematics in the same way as when we construct a machine.” Geometry, movement, mathematics, Duchamp’s massive impact on art history includes profoundly anticipating digital generative art well.

body: One of the key radical movements in modern art, abstraction and digital generative art history, Kazimir Malevich’s use of geometric forms and limited colors in Suprematism has had a profound impact on art history. Malevich believed that Suprematism was “the culmination (in Russia at least) of Futurism’s interest in dynamism and Cubism’s reduced geometric forms.” Suprematism greatly influenced contemporary generative art’s abstract geometric aesthetic, particularly early computer art. Malevich would not display the work he was creating during this period until 1915.

This revolutionary work of 1913 and 1914 remains one of the most famous examples of the use of chance in the history of art. Duchamp employed chance operations by dropping three one-meter threads, allowing them to take on random forms. He then traced and mounted these shapes as a commentary on the limitations of standard measurement systems. Duchamp’s exploration of chance and random processes questioned fundamental ideas such as artistic control and authorship, foreshadowing Dada as well as the embrace of generative algorithms in art creation. Crucially, his work gave legitimacy and recognition for chance operations in art, opening up possibilities for generative art and its algorithmic processes. This was part of Duchamp’s larger impact on conceptualism and shifting the focus from the artist’s hand to the underlying systems and concepts. This work, in the MoMA permanent collection, is thus one of the most foundation to this story of generative art history.

body: Inspired by technological and mechanical innovations of the time, this key work of the Orphism movement sought to explore the effects of color and light in abstract art. Delaunay’s masterful command of color and her pioneering use of abstraction would prove to be enduringly influential.

A seminal moment in art history, this exhibition showcased Malevich’s Black Square, Dynamic Suprematism and other abstract works that rejected traditional representational art, marking the birth of the Suprematist movement. Suprematism’s exultation of pure form and geometry would become fundamental aspects of digital generative art.

This work of the Russian avant-garde, painted in 1915 though dated 1913 by Malevich, remains one of art history’s cornerstones. Black Square was instrumental in establishing “a new world of shapes and forms” that would eventually lead to digital generative art. This radical rejection of representation in art is one of the first instances of pure abstraction in painting. The lasting symbol of Malevich’s career and Suprematism, Black Square was an earth-shattering work, radically challenging thousands of years of artistic tradition and marking a turning point in the history of art.

By emphasizing chance, randomness and absurdity in art, Dada stands as a foundational movement in the development of digital generative art. Writer Hugo Ball and the poet and performer Emmy Hennings founded Dadaism in the midst of WWI’s disillusionment from their satirical nightclub in Zurich, the Cabaret Voltaire. From there he published a magazine in which Ball wrote, “will bear the name ‘Dada’. Dada, Dada, Dada, Dada.” Frank Popper acknowledged Dada, along with Constructivism and Futurism, as one of the first quarter of the twentieth century’s three most important movements. Dada eventually formed the basis of Surrealism, Conceptual art, Neo-Dada, Fluxus and the chance elements of generative art. It’s impact cannot be overstated.
This Early Modern oil on canvas was completed during Mondrian’s transition from Cubism to Neoplasticism.
A. Michael Noll in 1965 would go on to conduct a famous early computer art experiment with Mondrian’s Composition with Lines.

He asked colleagues their preference between the Mondrian piece and his computer-created Computer Composition With Lines. This was an early attempt to compare the creative hand of the artist to the creative power of a machine.
Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll (transcript).

Founded by Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg originally as a publication, De Stijl means style in Dutch. It is believed that this magazine, De Stijl, was the first time the term “neo-plasticism” was used. The De Stijl movement sought to achieve a harmonious and universal visual language through the use of reduced geometric forms and primary colors. The movement’s emphasis on simplicity, primary colors and abstraction has resonated throughout generative art’s history. In addition to a clear aesthetic influence, De Stijl’s emphasis on grids and modular systems would impact future generations of generative artists.

body: The book by Scottish mathematical biologist D’Arcy Thompson showed how mathematical transformations could describe a variety of organic forms. Thompson thus pioneered the use of mathematics in biology which helped move forward mathematics in art. D’Arcy’s work greatly impacted computer art’s aesthetic in the second half of the century, particularly the artificial life movement.

body: Considered by many to be the first conceptual artwork, a key predecessor of digital generative art, this ready-made of a urinal remains one of the most important works in twentieth century art. Fountain exemplifies the irreverence of Dada and continues to influence any Deleuzian art form that challenges traditional conventions

This piece’s use of chance demonstrates an early example of an artist relinquishing control to challenge traditional art production techniques. Arp supposedly allowed random processes to determine the placement of the squares on the canvas. This act and the similar work of Duchamp marked a departure from traditional artistic control, serving as an early example of the element of randomness as a creative force. Arp’s work challenged the notion of the artist as a sole creator and laid the foundation for later developments in generative art, where algorithms and computational systems generate artworks. This piece remains foundational conceptually to not only Dadaism but to Surrealism and generative art.

body: Helping to introduce Cubism and Futurism into Russian art after visits to France and Italy before WWI, this piece is part of a series that demonstrates Popova’s Suprematist style. Popova, a pioneer of geometric abstraction and Suprematism, treated planes “like solid material entities,” laying them atop one another to create a radically new artistic language. Around fifteen years later, this layered-plane style would reemerge as Concrete art.

body: The publication of Après le Cubisme (After Cubism) began the Purism movement, proposing “a kind of painting in which objects are represented as powerful basic forms stripped of detail.” Purism relates to electronic and digital generative art due to its embrace of technology and a timeless machine aesthetic.

A canonical artefact of art history and one of the most important pieces of furniture ever built, the chair, designed in 1918 and painted about 1923, composed of 13 square-profiled battens, two rectangular panels and two armrests, was stripped of its volume to emphasize functionality. It stands as a representation of the De Stijl movement’s principles of abstract simplicity and functionality.

body: The revolutionary art school aimed to bring art into contact with everyday life, leveling the distinction between fine and applied art. It was formed by Walter Gropius after he succeeded Henry van de Velde as the head of the Weimar School of Arts and Crafts. This school, as the name implies, was heavily influenced by the British Arts & Crafts movement of the late nineteenth century. Instructors included modern art titans, including Anni and Josef Albers, Gunta Stölzl, Wassily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, László Moholy-Nagy and Johannes Itten. The school, which would become heavily influenced by the ideas of Constructivism due to Moholy-Nagy and Kandinsky in particular, emphasized the integration of art with design and technology. Bauhaus teachings also encouraged experimentation, with new materials and techniques. These principles laid the foundation for the development of not only modern art and design but generative art as well. Additionally, the school’s approach to abstract geometric forms as well as the reduction of art to its essential elements have influenced generative art’s aesthetics. Finally, the Bauhaus’s progressive and holistic approach to art education along with its focus on the fusion of art and craft had a lasting impact on art and technology.

body: Along with Fountain, this Dada classic of a crude comment below the Mona Lisa on which Duchamp drew a mustache and beard, remains a classic example of irreverence towards traditional art. Although Duchamp never associated himself with any particular movement, his legacy has impacted several; in this case, its Dada.

T.S. Eliot publishes “Tradition and the Individual Talent,” a critical essay that argues for greater understanding of the influence of canonical texts on any single writer and seeks to place the personality of the poet within a far greater tradition of literary voices and cultural ideas – prescient concepts that suggest ways in which AI may become valuable to writers. Three years later, in 1922, T.S. Eliot publishes The Waste Land, a landmark poem that freely interpolates material from a wealth of external sources, anticipating the synthesizing powers of large language models and deeply influencing the automated writing techniques of authors such as William Burroughs.
-Sasha Stiles

An early example of Lumino-kinetic art, progenitor of electronic art, this piece consisted of painted glass plates rotating on an electric motor to create optical illusions. One of Ray’s and Duchamp’s experiments with machines and motion, Rotary Glass Plates shattered traditional notions that art had to be static. It also questioned optical perception, an important predecessor to the Op Art movement.

A pivotal moment in the history of avant-garde art, the First International Dada-Fair showcased Dada’s anti-art and anti-establishment philosophy of absurdity and provocation to the world for the first time. It featured works from some of Dada’s most prominent participants, including Hans Arp, Max Ernst and Hannah Höch.

body: Along with Constructivists Rodchenko and Tatlin, Ray pioneered the use of mobiles (this one composed of 63 coat hangers), paving the way for future kinetic art and eventually all electronic art. This moment serves as a key example in art’s impulse towards kineticism in the early twentieth century. Artists, in an attempt to break free from the restraints of the static canvas, pushed to make art more dynamic and interactive, a huge leap along the path towards digital art.

This was the only workshop available to the women students at Bauhaus as all other workshops, from wood to metal, were open only to male students, and the Bauhaus had no architecture course until 1927.

body: Possibly the most influential among the avant-garde experimentalist giants, Tzara says in his own words, in a 1920 manifesto later collected in Seven Dada Manifestos:

"Take a newspaper. Take a pair of scissors. Choose an article as long as you are planning to make your poem. Cut out the article. Then cut out each of the words that make up this article and put them in a bag. Shake it gently. Then take out the scraps one after another in the order in which they left the bag. Copy conscientiously. The poem will be like you. And here you are a writer, infinitely original and endowed with a sensibility that is charming beyond the understanding of the vulgar."
Burroughs spoke of its influence on him in “The Third Mind interview” (1977) as have many others.
-Vuk Ćosić

body: Named by 1921 and led by Vladimir Tatlin and Alexander Rodchenko, Constructivism is arguably the most influential movement of the first half of the 20th c. on digital and generative art.
Influenced by Picasso’s Cubist constructions and the techo-inspired Manifesto of Futurism, Tatlin and Rodchenko believed art should directly reflect the modern industrial world.

Besides its importance in the development of kinetic and electronic art, Constructivism was highly influential on early, particularly European, computer art and Herbert W. Franke. Franke recognized that Constructivism’s visual language of lines and basic geometric forms lent itself naturally to code-based and computational art. Franke wrote that “the aim of many supporters of constructivist tendencies - a rejection of the personal element; a crystal-clear, objective presentation; the maximum precision - can be realized by the computer in a hitherto unparalleled degree.”
Beyond Franke, computer pioneer researchgate.net:

“I (that is, Ernest Edmonds) had been committed to painting since my early-teenage years, strongly influenced by the constructivists. I started to use a computer in my artwork in 1968, when I wrote a program that searched for an arrangement, a layout, of a given set of picture elements.”
An example of the Constructivist machine aesthetic can be found in Auro Lecci’s computer-generated Slant One.

body: Master of form Georg Muche “swore never to take a thread in his hand: He did not want to be associated with the feminine aura of weaving.” This led to Gunta Stölzl and Benita Otte taking courses at a technical school to teach their fellow classmates the technical aspects of working a loom.

Characterized by ordered, geometric forms, the work was completed one year before Moholy-Nagy began teaching at the Bauhaus. “Moholy-Nagy’s appointment signalled a major shift in the school’s philosophy away from its earlier crafts ethos towards a closer alignment with the demands of modern industry, and a programme of simple design and unadorned functionalism.”

body: Lumia is an Lumino-kinetic art form invented by Wilfred and performed on a device called a clavilux or “color organ.” These compositions of light were infinitely changing and had the appearance of a colorful aurora borealis. Lumia made Wilfred one of the most famous American artists of the 1920s. He would continue perfecting his craft for decades and was exhibited at MoMA in the influential 15 Americans (1952). Wilfred’s work with light was decades ahead of its time, paving the way for electronic, video and digital generative art, including the work of Nam June Paik.

body: Rayographs, photographs made by placing objects directly on sensitized paper and exposing them to light reflected Dada’s interest in chance and the nonsensical. “The random objects leave behind a shadowy imprint that dissociates them from their original context.” These works stand as critical examples of early generative as well as experimental photography.

The Constructivist Bauhaus teacher’s most famous work, this avant-garde artistic dance transformed dancers into geometrical shapes. Schlemmer’s aesthetics would go to influence Japanese Jikken Kobo. The following year, Schlemmer was hired as master of form at the Bauhaus theater workshop. Due to the popularity of performance, as the ballet toured, it helped to spread the word of Bauhaus around the world.

Moholy-Nagy remained at the Bauhaus until 1928, where he focused on painting, lithographs, montage, assemblage and photography. The pioneer of experimental photography, heavily inspired in later years by the upcoming Constructivism, advocated for a fusion of art and technology. His ideas about the role of art in modern society influenced the development of the Bauhaus and subsequent modernist movements.

While at the Bauhaus, Kandinsky further developed his Constructivist aesthetic by investigating the use of color, form, and composition to convey emotional and spiritual themes. One of Kandinsky’s most well-known works, Composition 8 also presages the dominant role of circles in his later work.
Originally conceived of to unify arts and crafts, the Bauhaus under Gropius began pivoting to design for mass production, adopting the slogan “Art into Industry.”

body: Constructivism’s manifesto espoused the belief that art should directly reflect the modern industrial world: “The material formation of the object is to be substituted for its aesthetic combination. The object is to be treated as a whole and thus will be of no discernible ‘style’ but simply a product of an industrial order like a car, an aeroplane and such like. Constructivism is a purely technical mastery and organisation of materials.” Constructivism emphasized the integration of art and technology, seeking to create practical, functional objects that embodied the principles of modern industrial society. These ideas would also prove hugely influential to the Bauhaus. Tatlin aimed to bridge the gap between art and everyday life, embracing materials such as metal, glass, and other industrial materials. Constructivism focused on the notion of art as a social and political force for change, emphasizing collective creativity and the importance of utility and construction.

Led by Tomoyoshi Murayama, this radical Japanese art movement promulgated an interdisciplinary array of performance art, painting, illustration and architecture to communicate anti-establishment messages to the mainstream. Reacting to Japan’s rapid modernization and industrial development, the Mavo group’s works focused on crisis, peril and uncertainty. Mavo sought to reintegrate art into daily life, a concept predating New Tendencies and GRAV by 40 years. Mavo thus was critical to the advancement of audience participation in art, an important concept in digital art.

One of the most important predecessors of generative art due to its use of chance, Breton called for artists to bypass reason and rationality by accessing their unconscious mind. Contemporary language artist, Sasha Stiles details its importance: “The French poet, critic and editor André Breton publishes the Surrealist Manifesto, in which he lays the groundwork for subsequent automated and aleatory writing techniques by defining Surrealism as ‘Psychic automatism in its pure state, by which one proposes to express…the actual functioning of thought…in the absence of any control exercised by reason, exempt from any aesthetic or moral concern.’”

body: The signature work of van Doesburg features a simple composition of geometric shapes and colors arranged in a dynamic and asymmetrical pattern. The piece exemplifies the principles of De Stijl, seeking to create a universal language of form and color that could be applied to all aspects of art and design.

A critical publication by the leaders of the Dadaist and Constructivist movements documenting the turbulent developemtns of the art world in the first quarter of the twentieth century. The book opens with definitions of each movement by leading artists, followed by photographic plates surveying the isms of 1914 to 1924, among them Dadaism, Constructivism and Futurism. It serves as a visual exploration and representation of the diverse artistic movements of the early 20th century, showcasing their different ideologies and aesthetics.

body: One of the most important developments in digital and generative art’s history, Bell Labs would go on to become instrumental in the development of computational art and animation. The list of pioneering engineers and artists with connections to the Lab is astonishing. The list includes: Billy Klüver, Kenneth Knowlton, A. Michael Noll, Béla Julesz, Edward Zajec, Leon Harmon, Claude Shannon, Stan Vanderbeek, Lillian Schwartz, Nam June Paik and Max Mathews.

Their innovative work in the 1960s and 1970s was absolutely critical to the development of art and technology, laying the groundwork for the digital art revolution that would follow. In fact, Bell Labs’s Billy Klüver would co-found Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.) with Robert Rauschenberg in the ’60s.
Listen to Peter Bauman’s interview with A. Michael Noll (transcript).

A key event in the fusion of art and industry, the exhibition saw avant-garde ideas from around the globe presented for the first time. It was instrumental to the development of modern design and architecture. The term Art Deco derives from this exhibition but was only coined in the 1960s.

body: Moving from Weimar to Dessau, this Walter Gropius designed building for the Bauhaus was envisioned as a “Gesamtkunstwerk” (comprehensive artwork). “The building contained many features that later became hallmarks of modernist architecture, including steel-frame construction, a glass curtain wall, and an asymmetrical, pinwheel plan,” according to the Met.

Following the move to Dessau, the weaving workshop relocated to a large studio with new looms. With Georg Muche, the workshop’s master of form, lacking the knowledge to operate the new equipment, the weavers demanded Gunta Stölzl take over. The demand led to unrest throughout the school and a reexamining of the masters.

Based on parlor games, the group began creating “exquisite corpses,” which involved collaborative and random creations based on a set of rules. This technique was a precursor to rules-based systems producing random results.

body: Made head of workshop in 1927 and formally Jungmeister in 1928, holding the post until 1931, Stölzl became the first woman to fill a senior position at the Bauhaus due to the wide support of her students. It was after Stölzl took charge of the workshop that its importance and innovation increased.

One of the most important theoretical sources in the development of abstract art, the book articulated the principles of Suprematism, which rejected representation in favor of pure abstraction. Suprematism sought to transcend materiality and represent the spiritual essence of art. Malevich advocated for non-objective art, stripping down forms to their basic geometric elements, primarily focusing on squares, circles and lines. Suprematism aimed to evoke a sense of pure aesthetic experience, emphasizing the supremacy of pure feeling and perception over representational content. The book articulates Malevich’s rejection of utilitarianism and focus on the exploration of geometric abstraction as a means to access universal truths and transcend the physical world. In contrast to Malevich’s Suprematism, Tatlin’s Constructivism aimed to combine art with utility, integrating art and technology. Constructivists sought to create practical, functional objects that embodied the principles of modern industrial society. While Constructivism emphasized functionality, industrial materials and the integration of art and society, Suprematism embraced non-objectivity, geometric abstraction and the pursuit of spiritual and universal truths.

body: A fundamental development in the inclusion of chance in abstract art, grattage involves scraping or scratching the surface of a canvas covered with layers of paint, revealing the textures and patterns created by the different layers. Ernst used this experimental technique in his surrealist paintings, allowing chance and improvisation to guide the creation of the final image.

body: One of the most celebrated and prolific inventors of all time, Farnsworth was the quintessential “mad scientist” and inspiration for Professor Farnsworth on TV series Futruama. His “image dissector” was an early television transmission tube that focused light on a detector in front of a tube, which could convert electrons into electrical signals visible by a television receiver. This tube was also the center of a longstanding legal battle between Farnsworth and RCA over the invention of the television. While Farnsworth won the battle, RCA ended up winning the war in the long run despite technology inferior to Farnsworhth’s.

Mentioned in the Cybernetic Serendipity catalog as an important development in the history of cybernetics, the Differential Analyser was an early mechanical computer, invented by the American engineer, used to solve complex mathematical problems. With rotating gears and shafts, it performed calculations and allowed researchers to model physical phenomena such as the motion of planets and the behavior of fluids. Bush’s invention had a significant impact on cybernetic devices and the development of modern computers.

Under new director Hannes Meyer, women at the Bauhaus are allowed to choose their own workshops and admitted to study architecture. This long-overdue step towards greater gender inclusivity meant that the women students were no longer confined to the weaving workshop only.

body: Highways and Byways, a painting by the Swiss artist Paul Klee, is significant for its synthesis of Klee’s interests in geometric abstraction and music. Klee uses color to evoke a sense of movement and rhythm. It represents a high point in Klee’s career and exemplifies the artist’s innovative approach to painting, which influenced generations of artists in the 20th century, including Vera Molár.

body: A work which presages the mathematics-based, geometric compositions of contemporary generative art, van Doesburg’s piece stands as an example of the De Stijl movement’s attempt to create a new visual language based on geometric forms and primary colors. Its diagonal composition reflects van Doesburg’s interest in the relationship between art and technology.

One of the first electrically powered kinetic sculptures, this kinetic light sculpture is an important example of the historical lineage connecting early Lumino-Kinetic Art to Op and Kinetic art, which led to the development of digital art. Created two years after Moholy-Nagy left the Bauhaus, this piece synthesizes his experiments there, incorporating light, technology and industrial materials.

It represents a shift towards abstraction and a rejection of naturalism in art, becoming a seminal work in the development of abstract art and modernism.

body: Gunta Stölzl, pioneering weaver and textile artist, left the Bauhaus due to conflicts with its male-dominated administration, her support for left-wing politics and rising anti-semitism in Germany. Her departure was a significant loss for the school but Stölzl would continue to be a leading figure in the development of modernist textile art and design. She would become the first woman to be exhibited for textiles at MoMA.

body: The Nazis permanently closed Bauhaus due to their opposition to its modernist and internationalist principles, which they saw as incompatible with their vision of a “pure” and traditional German culture. body: Black Mountain College was founded in North Carolina as an experimental liberal arts college with a focus on the arts, including music, visual arts, and creative writing. It became a seminal institution in the development of modernist art and education, hosting influential artists and thinkers such as John Cage, Anni and Josef Albers, Cy Twombly and Robert Rauschenberg. Several former Bauhaus faculty members, such as the Alberses, joined the Black Mountain College faculty. The college adopted many of the Bauhaus’s principles of interdisciplinary collaboration, experimentation, and the integration of art and technology.

Vera Molnar saw this piece and was encouraged to create her own abstract, constructivist-inspired art, the computer art pioneer told Hans Ulrich Obrist. A vibrant and dynamic abstract painting, Hélion’s work was a challenge to traditional notions of representation and perspective.

His new style was known as Universalismo Constructivo (Constructive Universalism) and aimed to inject emotion and humanity into the austere aesthetics of De Stijl and Constructivism.

A paramount work in the intersection of chance and art, The Green Box consists of ninety-four loose documents that all related to the idea of chance. body: A groundbreaking event in the history of abstraction and modernism in North America, this exhibition developed the narrative that adventurous artists were rejecting representation due to having grown “bored with painting facts.” The exhibition marked a shift in the global center of the art world from Europe to New York. This trend would dramatically accelerate during and after WWII, which was in its early phases in Asia. This instrumental exhibition’s weight can still be felt today as the narrative it created (proposed by MoMA’s founding director Alfred H. Barr, Jr.) continues to shape how modernism is presented.

body: Zuse would finish the motor-driven, mechanical computer in 1938. The first freely programmable binary computer, the Z1 laid the groundwork for modern computers by using Boolean logic and incorporating program control. The Z1 used moving rods and plates to represent 1s and 0s, reading instructions from punched tape.

body: This influential paper holds immense importance in the development of artificial intelligence (AI), showing that neural networks could perform logical operations and suggested that the brain might work like a digital computer. The paper presented a formal model of neural networks, demonstrating how complex cognitive processes could be understood through logical and mathematical principles. Their work proved foundational to the field of computational neuroscience, inspiring subsequent research in AI and machine learning. By bridging the gap between biology and computation, McCulloch and Pitts provided a framework for simulating intelligent behavior, influencing the development of AI algorithms and architectures. In papers from 1945-1952, McCulloch and Pitts would continue developing the mathematical theory of the mind.

body: Kepes, an artist, designer and theoretician, analyzes the effect of visual language on the structure of human consciousness. The book’s explored the concept of visual language and how elements such as line, color and form could be used to create new visual structures. In addition to influencing the post-war Japanese avant-garde, the book also provided a theoretical foundation for the creation of generative art. It outlined principles of composition as well as encouraging experimentation and innovation with basic forms, a task perfectly suited to algorithmic art.

body: Termed “an essential document in the bibliography of 20th-century history” by Jorge Glusberg, the modest abstract art magazine’s first and only issue in 1944 was printed in the Buenos Aires Caballito district. The single issue, with a cover by Tomás Maldonado, is credited for birthing both the Asociación Arte Concreto-Invención (AACI) in 1945 as well as Gyula Kosice’s Madí in 1946. Both groups were inspired by the prominently featured work of Joaquin Torres García, founder of Latin American Constructivism, as well as the magazine’s advocacy for the societal benefits of geometric art.

body: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), unveiled in February 1946, was the prototype from which modern computers evolved. Developed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert of the University of Pennsylvania, ENIAC is commonly called the first general-purpose electronic and digital computer. Laying the foundation for modern computing, ENIAC demonstrated that high-speed digital computing was possible with vacuum tubes. Considered “the first digital computer, [it] weighed over thirty tons, consumed 200 kilowatts of electrical power, and contained around 19,000 vacuum tubes that got very hot very fast, and as a result constantly burned out, making it very unreliable.” Commissioned in 1943, ENIAC was financed by the United States Army, Ordnance Corps during WWII to calculate artillery firing tables. Thus, the history of computing coincides with the military and warfare, which will continue for the several decades. It would not be until the late 1970s that computers would lose the air of mystery and fear that largely surrounded them with the advent of personal computers and video games.

Famously it was six women who programmed it, known as the ENIAC Six: Kathleen McNulty, Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman. They set up the trajectory calculation shown at the February 1946 unveiling despite not even being introduced at the event.

body: Veronika “Vera” Gács arrived in Paris on December 10, 1947, with her soon-to-be husband, François Molnár. “I was obsessed with the desire to see modern art, and for me that could only mean Paris,” she later recalled.1 The twenty-three-year-old Vera stayed with François at a hotel on Rue de l’Hirondelle, her first place of residence in the city. There she would produce her first creative expression in Paris, drawing the house across the street from her hotel window. body: Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics was published the same year as Claude Shannon’s "A Mathematical Theory of Communication.” Max Bense would apply both their works to aesthetics in his pioneering work, Aesthetica (1965), which laid the theoretical foundations of digital and AI art with computer art.

Cybernetics thus played a vital role in both the birth of digital art and artificial intelligence, thus making it one of the single most important moments on the timeline. Max Bense and his role at the University of Stuttgart explains the connection to computer art, specifically. He taught the first European computer artists, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake, leaving an indelible marks on their thinking that last to this day, as this 2018 talk by Nake demonstrates.

For artificial intelligence, cybernetics was an early attempt to unite machines and organic beings in a functional way, as it sought a theory of control, feedback and communication applicable to machines as well as animals. In the book Art in the Age of Machine Learning, author Sofian Audry argues that the concept of machine learning dates back to cybernetics.
According to the writer Jack Burnham, curator of the legendary Software exhibition:
“One of the landmarks in the history of science occurred in 1947 when the M.I.T. mathematician Norbert Wiener along with his colleague Arture Rosenblueth of Harvard, coined the word Cybernetics.”

Max Bense would apply both their works to aesthetics in his pioneering work, Aesthetica (1965), which laid the theoretical foundations of digital and AI art with computer art.

Written at Bell Labs, Shannon’s paper “defined in mathematical terms what information is and how it can be transmitted in the face of noise. What had been viewed as quite distinct modes of communication--the telegraph, telephone, radio and television--were unified in a single framework.”

The Molnárs had access to a studio on the estate, which delighted the young artists and made their visiting artist friends extremely jealous. body: Asger Jorn organized CoBrA with Karel Appel, Constant, Corneille, the writer Christian Dotremont and Joseph Noiret; Pierre Alechinsky joined the following year. Named after the first letters of the capitals of the founders’ home countries (Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam), CoBrA rejected rationality, individualism and classicism in art. Embracing collaboration and Surrealism, CoBrA also rejected the notion of the lone-genius artist, a stance echoed in the following decade by Victor Vasarely and GRAV.

body: More commonly referred to as Yomiuri Anpan, the annual non-juried exhibition played a crucial role in the birth of Japanese postwar avant-garde art. Famously democratizing, anyone could show their work by paying the fee in an attempt to promote freedom of expression and thought. Supervised by Japanese Surrealist icon Shuzo Takiguchi, instrumental in the formation of Jikken Kobo, Yomiuri Anpan offered an ideal space for independent artists and the most experimental works (even judged by today’s standards).

body: The Boolean binary logic that underpins all of computation and thus contemporary society traces back to this 1854 book.

George Boole published An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, while professor of mathematics at Queen's College, Cork. Largely self-taught, he stated his aim in the first sentence: “to investigate the fundamental laws of those operations of the mind by which reasoning is performed; to give expression to them in the symbolical language of a Calculus.” He treated logic as algebra over two values, 1 and 0, true and false. In 1937 Claude Shannon's master's thesis showed that switching circuits obey Boole's algebra, and digital computers have been built on it ever since.

body: For further proof that our fear of producing intelligent machines that could one day overtake us is nothing new, see Samuel Butler's satirical novel Erewhon; or, Over the Range.

In the book, its narrator finds a hidden country whose people destroyed every machine invented in the previous 271 years, persuaded by a book that noticed machines were evolving faster than living things and might one day become conscious. Ring a bell?

body: There have always been twin views on technology and where it's leading us. Even a hundred years ago writers like H. G. Wells wrote of tech utopias while E. M. Forster was decidedly less optimistic.

In Forster's story “The Machine Stops,” humanity lives underground in identical rooms, each person's needs met by a global Machine. This immediately recalls contemporary futuristic visions of this dystopia, like Fallout and Silo.

It also eerily predicted more contemporary afflictions like video calls and blackboxes, as in Forster's story people rarely meet; they talk through screens and trade ideas second hand. When the Machine begins to fail and no one remembers how to repair it, a religion grows up around its manual. At least we have something to look forward to.

body: Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo built the chess-playing automaton, El Ajedrecista (The Chess Player), in 1912 and presented it in Paris in 1914.

Incapable of playing a full game from scratch, the machine played one specific endgame, its own king and rook against a human’s lone king. It could sense the pieces electrically and move its own with a mechanical arm. A 1915 Scientific American account reported Quevedo's claim that “an automaton can do many things that are popularly classed with thought.” A second version, built in 1920, moved the pieces with electromagnets under the board.

This machine would even impact the budding field of cybernetics, when in January 1951 Quevedo's son Gonzalo Torres-Quevedo presented both machines at a Paris conference, where the 1920 machine defeated none other than Norbert Wiener.

body: It was around this time that automaton started losing the verbal fight with the term, a hundred years later, we still use today: robot. And to be honest, not a great start for our relationship.

Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) was published in Prague in November 1920 and first staged in January 1921. Its robots are artificial workers made from synthetic organic matter and built to free people from labor. Ah but they rebel and wipe out humanity.

The word robot came from the Czech robota, forced labor. In proof that art is always relevant (wink), Karel credited his brother, the painter Josef Čapek, with suggesting the name. It would take several years for the word to gain widespread acknowledgement let alone popularity. In 1922 the play had gone to New York and was in London in 1923, along with an English translation. From there, the word spread from English into dozens of other languages. And here we are today still using it.

body: Hedy Lamarr was one of Golden Age Hollywood's most sought after stars. But she was also an inventor. With all hands on deck during WWII on August 11, 1942, Lamarr and composer George Antheil received a US patent for a “Secret Communication System.”

Known as frequency-hopping, the technique kept radio-guided torpedoes from being jammed. The transmitter and receiver would jump together between 88 frequencies, synchronized like a player piano. Although ultimately not used during the war, frequency hopping later became relevant with wireless communication. As such, Lamarr entered the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2014.

body: The roots of cybernetics lie uncomfortably in the terrain of autonomous weapons and the military industrial complex. After all, the ideas grew smack in the middle of WWII.
In January 1943 Arturo Rosenblueth of Harvard Medical School, Norbert Wiener of MIT and Julian Bigelow published “Behavior, Purpose and Teleology” in Philosophy of Science.
Working on anti-aircraft fire control, Wiener and Bigelow conclude that voluntary action depends on feedback.

The essay applied one scheme to animals and machines, citing a target-seeking torpedo: “All purposeful behavior may be considered to require negative feed-back.” Rosenblueth supplied the medical parallel, a patient with cerebellar disease whose hand oscillates more and more as it carries a glass of water to his mouth. He had presented the ideas at a 1942 Macy Foundation meeting in New York attended by Warren McCulloch.

One of technology's original sins which this moment highlights is the inexorable tie between technology and weapons. It's all the more unsettling how long we've been trying to make weapons more responsive and lifelike.

body: Assembly language, a complex computational layer just above binary that every higher-level language leverages, is thus foundational. Along with the ENIAC Six, another often overlooked woman in the history of programming is the English mathematician Kathleen Booth.

At Birkbeck College in London, Booth worked with husband Andrew Donald Booth on their Automatic Relay Calculator, writing Coding for A.R.C. in 1947. It set out a symbolic notation for instructions that stood between the programmer and the machine's raw numbers and counted among the first assembly languages. The Booths went on to build the APE(X)C computers in the early 1950s, with Kathleen Booth later writing one of the first books on programming, Programming for an Automatic Digital Calculator (1958).

body: Machines leveraging chance with stored programs, the roots actually extend to just after WWII with the story of Klára Dán von Neumann.

Besides how often overlooked early women programmers were, the story of Klára Dán von Neumann also reminds us (again and again) of the uncomfortable and unrelenting connection between computers and the military, including weapons as unsavory as the atomic variety.

In the spring of 1948 Klára Dán von Neumann (wife of John von Neumann) wrote and ran the code for a series of Monte Carlo simulations of nuclear chain reactions for Los Alamos on ENIAC. The machine had only just been converted to run programs stored in memory. The method, devised by Stanisław Ulam and John von Neumann with Nicholas Metropolis, answered questions too complex to calculate directly by following thousands of random paths and counting the outcomes. Her programs were among the first to use a modern, stored-program design. Chance put to work by a machine, the same principle runs through generative art from Georg Nees, Vera Molnár and onward.

body: Norbert Wiener, the MIT mathematician whose significance is covered extensively on this timeline, published Cybernetics: or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine in 1948. Cybernetics as a term comes from the Greek for steersman, and named a science of feedback. It described how systems, living or mechanical, measure the effects of their actions and correct themselves. Wiener drew on his wartime work on anti-aircraft prediction, mentioned previously in this Timeline and on meetings with Warren McCulloch, Walter Pitts, John von Neumann and others.

The impact of cybernetics on computation and AI is foundational to both. So, it's pretty important. For art, its ideas reached artists through Max Bense in Stuttgart and Jasia Reichardt's 1968 exhibition Cybernetic Serendipity.

body: From the history of automatons to early robots, but especially around this time post WWII, people started dreaming of "Thinking Machines." Not just "mindless" instruction followers but machines capable of their own thought like the human brain. That includes adaptability. The homeostat was one of the first devices capable of adaptation by mimicking supposed brain functions by reaching equilibrium with pivoting magnets.

At Barnwood House, a psychiatric hospital in Gloucester, England, W. Ross Ashby and his laboratory assistant Denis Bannister completed the homeostat in March 1948 from four ex-RAF bomb control units. Again we see technology and war's close ties. Ashby himself was a central figure of the post-war British cyberneticists.

Each unit carried a pivoted magnet and fed its output to the other three. When a magnet swung too far, a stepping switch gave its unit new circuit values, drawn from a table of random numbers, until all four magnets settled at the center again. Ashby called this ultrastability. In January 1949 Time called the machine “the closest thing to a synthetic brain so far designed by man.” Ashby set out the theory in Design for a Brain (1952).

While the homeostat's complicated and esoteric functioning no longer persists mechanically, the ideas that the machine pointed to would become some of the most relevant and important in the decades to today.

body: It was around this mid-century turn in history when the advancements in neuroscience provided scientists in many different fields, a better understanding of the inner-workings of the human brain, neurons. This is critical because science and technology influence each other. And this work would provide future computer scientists (see Rosenblatt below) a brain-based model on which to inspire their work.

The paper itself was by McGill University psychologist Donald O. Hebb, who published The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory. He proposed that when one nerve cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, some growth process or metabolic change makes the first more efficient at firing the second. Frequently repeated stimulation would build groups of such cells, which he called cell assemblies, and he described a series of their actions as the thought process.

Early AI researcher Frank Rosenblatt named Hebb’s work as an inspiration for his 1958 perceptron. The slogan “cells that fire together, wire together” came later, from the neurobiologist Carla Shatz in a 1992 Scientific American article.
